q: Do the ten 190-bp repeated elements (5 per replichore, in-orientation with the replication fork) function as structural non-coding RNAs, cis-encoded replication-directional signals, or degenerate mobile-element scars — and does that assignment hold when the same analysis is redone on RefSeq NC_000964.3 with modern structural-RNA and Rfam/CMscan tools?
basis: Kunst et al. (1997) called out this 190-bp × 10 element as the most prominent duplication in the genome, noted conserved secondary structure via compensatory mutations, and hypothesized a structural RNA role, but left its identity open. This replication showed the analytical claim (C17) is testable in principle but was not attempted — it is exactly the kind of concrete, bounded structural-genomics problem that would clarify a persistent 28-year-old paper mystery. No Rfam family (as of Rfam 14.x) is currently assigned to a 190-bp × 10 in-orientation element on the B. subtilis 168 chromosome, so this is genuinely open.
next_steps: 1) Extract the ten paper-nominated 190-bp windows from NC_000964.3 by MUMmer/self-BLAST (word≥24, e≤1e-10) and confirm the 6+3+1 subfamily structure. 2) Run Infernal/cmscan against Rfam 14.x on the ten copies plus flanks to test for an existing structural RNA hit. 3) Fold each copy with RNAfold/LinearFold and Bhattacharyya-compare the base-pairing probability matrices to confirm/deny compensatory conservation. 4) Cross-check strand vs replication direction with a fresh GC-skew-derived terminus rather than the paper's 2,017 kb prior. 5) Query B. subtilis 168 tiling-array + RNA-seq deposits (GEO/ArrayExpress) for expression signal at those coordinates. Success = a specific assignment (novel sRNA family, integrated-mobile-element footprint, or replication-directional cis-element) with supporting evidence at all four layers.

q: Do the three codon-usage classes (3,375 / 188 / 537 CDSs) claimed by factorial correspondence analysis in the paper survive as *statistically stable* clusters under modern unsupervised methods (UMAP, HDBSCAN, dirichlet-multinomial mixtures) on the current NC_000964.3 CDS set, and does class 3 continue to co-localize with A+T-rich islands / prophage-like regions when the CDS list has grown from ~4,100 to 4,237?
basis: This replication tested every whole-genome fractional metric but explicitly did NOT re-derive the paper's Class 1/2/3 codon partition (C18 in the claims table). The three-class picture drives a huge amount of downstream narrative in the paper (highly expressed vs prophage-derived vs housekeeping), and it was built with 1997-vintage factorial correspondence analysis. Whether the same three-cluster structure emerges from a 2020s method or dissolves into a continuum is genuinely unknown. It is also a good testbed for whether a well-cited but old clustering result is method-artefact or biology.
next_steps: 1) Extract all 4,237 CDSs from NC_000964.3, compute the 59-dimensional codon-usage vector (or RSCU) per CDS. 2) Replicate the paper's factorial correspondence analysis (Correspondance des Correspondances / R `ca` package) with the exact 1997-era parameters. 3) Re-cluster with three modern methods (UMAP + HDBSCAN; Dirichlet-multinomial mixture with BIC-selected K; SIMCA supervised against the paper's tRNA-abundance-defined highly-expressed set) and compare with Adjusted Rand Index and silhouette against the paper's 3-class labels. 4) Map recovered class-3 members against a current prophage annotation (PHASTER/PhiSpy on NC_000964.3) and A+T-rich islands. 5) Report whether K=3 is *supported* (BIC minimum at 3), whether membership is stable across methods, and whether class-3-vs-prophage co-localization is significant (permutation test). Success = a defensible modern answer to whether 3-class codon partitioning of B. subtilis is real.

q: How much of the CDS count drift (4,237 in NC_000964.3 today vs the paper's ~4,100 in 1997, ≈ +3.3%) is *newly discovered real coding sequence* (small ORFs, leader peptides, antisense ORFs, ribosome-profiling-validated smORFs) vs *annotation over-call* (spurious ORFs added in later rounds), and what is the correct present-day gene count for B. subtilis 168 when small-ORF and ribosome-profiling evidence are jointly required?
basis: The paper itself flagged this as an open problem ("the estimated number of B. subtilis CDSs will fluctuate around the present figure of 4,100... some of the short CDSs present in the B. subtilis genome have been overlooked"). This replication surfaced a +137 CDS drift (evidence/metrics.json: 4,237 vs 4,100) but did not adjudicate whether the extra CDSs are real. Recent smORF/ribosome-profiling work in B. subtilis (Fuchs et al., Meydan et al., 2018-2023) has identified dozens of previously missed short ORFs, but a unified reconciliation of the RefSeq annotation against ribosome-profiling evidence has not (to our knowledge) been published for the current NC_000964.3 annotation.
next_steps: 1) Diff the 1997 AL009126.1 CDS list vs the current NC_000964.3 CDS list — inventory gained, lost, and boundary-changed CDSs. 2) For every *new* CDS since 1997, test three evidence axes: (a) ribosome-profiling read coverage in public GEO B. subtilis Ribo-seq deposits (GSE99525, GSE104725, others), (b) MS/MS peptide support in ProteomicsDB / PRIDE B. subtilis reference proteome, (c) synteny + conservation across a curated set of ≥10 Bacillus species. 3) Score each new CDS on those axes and classify as ribosome-supported / MS-supported / conservation-only / unsupported. 4) Publish a curated 2026-vintage 'gold-standard' CDS list for B. subtilis 168 with per-CDS evidence tags. Success = a defensible present-day CDS count with per-CDS evidence attached.

q: Given the paper reports ~75% of CDSs co-oriented with the replication fork and this replication measured 73.0%, what is the true single-nucleotide-resolution terminus of B. subtilis 168 replication (rather than the paper's ~2,017 kb rounded prior), and does re-deriving the co-orientation fraction from a GC-skew-inferred terminus + high-resolution replichore assignment change the number in a way that resolves the paper-vs-replication delta?
basis: This replication (C15 + C16) explicitly used the paper's own 2,017 kb terminus as a prior instead of independently re-deriving it, and the failure_analysis lists this as an unverified shortcut. The paper's 75% figure is itself unrounded but based on 1997-era CDS boundaries. A modern GC-skew / z-curve terminus call on NC_000964.3, combined with the current CDS set, is a small, bounded, but honest closure of this loop, and is *exactly* the kind of second-order check the paper leaves implicit.
next_steps: 1) Compute cumulative GC skew (G-C)/(G+C) in 10-kb windows across NC_000964.3; locate the terminus by minimum of the cumulative skew. 2) Cross-check with the Ori/Ter prediction of Oriloc and z-curve method (Grigoriev, Chen & Zhang). 3) Recompute the co-orientation fraction with (a) the GC-skew terminus, (b) an assumed exact terminus at the *dif* site coordinates, (c) the paper's 2,017 kb, and report the sensitivity. 4) Break down co-orientation by class 1/2/3 codon usage class and by essentiality (per SubtiWiki) to see whether the ~25% counter-oriented set is enriched for non-essential, prophage-associated, or class 3 CDSs. Success = a fully-owned co-orientation number ± error bar for present-day NC_000964.3, and a defensible statement on whether the paper's 75% is an over-round or an under-count.

q: Which of the 1997-era 'y-gene' unknowns (paper: 42% of CDSs then had no functional assignment) remain unknown in 2026 after 28 years of homology, structure prediction (AlphaFold), and functional-genomics work, and does the *residual unknown fraction* concentrate in specific genomic regions (A+T islands, class-3 codon-usage regions, prophage boundaries, near the terminus) — i.e., is the *durable unknown* structurally biased?
basis: The paper's 58% functional-assignment fraction (C21 in the claims table) was explicitly not re-derived by this replication because it depends on the SWISS-PROT R34 vintage set. A modern re-run against UniRef/InterPro + a comprehensive AlphaFold-DB structural coverage analysis would produce a 2026 functional-assignment number. More interestingly, the DIFFERENCE between the 1997 and 2026 numbers, spatially resolved, would identify B. subtilis's most durable unknowns — the parts of the paradigm Gram-positive genome that resist all modern tools. This is directly actionable for follow-up functional work.
next_steps: 1) Snapshot the current NC_000964.3 CDS set (4,237 entries) and pull all current SubtiWiki / EcoCyc / UniProt functional annotations + GO evidence codes. 2) Re-run BLAST/DIAMOND vs UniRef50, HMMER/InterProScan vs Pfam-A + TIGRFAM + CDD, and structural search via AlphaFold-DB Foldseek against the entire PDB. 3) Score each CDS as one of {experimentally-characterized / homology-only / structure-only / hypothetical-supported / durable-unknown}. 4) Compute the 2026 'assigned function' fraction and diff against the paper's 58%. 5) Spatially plot durable-unknowns along the chromosome and test for enrichment in A+T islands, class-3 codon-usage regions, and prophage boundaries with a proper null model. 6) Publish a ranked shortlist of ≤50 top durable-unknowns as an experimental target list. Success = a mapped, spatially-resolved 'durable unknown' catalogue and a testable hypothesis about *where* function stays hidden in the B. subtilis paradigm genome.
